newsitem.title: UK: Don't blame milk for colicky babies - study.
newsitem.headline: Don't blame milk for colicky babies - study.

text.p: Changing a baby's infant formula will probably do little to deal with the problem of colic -- the constant crying that drives parents mad -- doctors said on Friday.
A British study of more than 76,000 babies and their parents showed age and social class had more to do with perceptions of colic than anything else.
There was no evidence that colicky or fussy babies were any less healthy.
David Strachan and colleagues at St George's Hospital Medical School in London analysed interviews made of the mothers of the 76,000 babies, born between 1975 and 1988.
The interviews were done in a study of cot death (sudden infant death syndrome) but included questions about colic -- usually defined as excessive crying for no apparent reason.
About 12,000 of the babies were reported as colicky.
Colicky babies slept less -- or so it seemed to parents -- and were slightly more likely to be breast-fed, the report, published in the British Medical Journal, said.
But Strachan said switching the baby to formula, or from one formula to another, did nothing to help.

"Parents were obviously experimenting to see what affected their baby's colic," Strachan said in a telephone interview. "That's quite an important public health message because we don't want parents to be pushed into stopping breast-feeding."
He added: "What we thought was the more interesting finding was the fact that so few of the biological factors we addressed, such as birthweight, were unrelated to colic."
Strachan said he was concerned that people might conclude from the report that some parents simply noticed crying more than others.
"We might be accused of saying that parents were either over-anxious or under-anxious about their child's crying."
He said more objective studies would have to be done, with parents keeping careful note of how long a baby spent crying, sleeping or calmly resting.
But Strachan said the consequences of colic could be serious.
"If you speak to psychologists they tell you all about the importance of early bonding between infant and mother, and if the infant is not playing ball, it could have consequences," he said.
